title: This Year We Can End the Death Penalty in California

title: Programming Bottom-Up
candidate_workflows: Build a product's internal language alongside the product: extract recurring operators, reuse them across components, and repeatedly redraw the boundary between generic infrastructure and application-specific code.
Use abstraction to reduce components and connections so a small technical team can move faster with fewer coordination and defect surfaces.

title: Chapter 2 of Ansi Common Lisp
candidate_workflows: Work incrementally at an interactive top level: write a function, call it to test it, inspect the returned value, and use immediate feedback to correct behavior before continuing.
Reduce side effects so functions remain independently testable, preserve short change-to-feedback cycles, and adapt the language or abstractions to fit the program as it evolves.

title: Chapter 1 of Ansi Common Lisp
candidate_workflows: Choose tools and architecture that shorten correction cycles; prototype before completing a specification, let implementation experience reshape the design, and evolve the working prototype toward production.
Separate general from specific by building reusable lower layers and keeping application-specific behavior in the top layer.

title: Lisp for Web-Based Applications
exclusion_reason: The local document only introduces and links to external talk excerpts about Viaweb's Lisp implementation; it contains no substantive workflow to audit or reuse.

title: Beating the Averages
candidate_workflows: Select technology by the leverage it creates for this product rather than by popularity; state a falsifiable advantage hypothesis, then test whether it improves feature speed, product capability, team size, and cost.
Protect a hard-to-copy technical advantage while users experience its benefits, and reveal as little implementation detail to competitors as the market requires.
Evaluate software competitors through working demos and specific hiring requirements, using those concrete signals to infer technical depth and development speed.

title: Java's Cover
candidate_workflows: Triage an unfamiliar technology before investing deeply by checking whether adoption is voluntary, expert users love it, creators built it for themselves, governance stays small and coherent, and sponsor incentives align with user value.
Treat hype, forced adoption, bureaucratic process, committee ownership, and dependence on a struggling sponsor as warning signals to investigate rather than as proof of quality.

title: Being Popular
candidate_workflows: Choose a demanding target user, learn what that user needs from real work, and bootstrap initial adoption by attaching the new capability to an application people already want.

Start with a small working version, keep early users few enough for close contact, improve from their demanding feedback, and repeat the product story long enough for the market to notice persistence.
Alternate confident building with skeptical redesign; delay broad growth when compatibility pressure would prevent correcting the product's foundations.

title: Five Questions about Language Design
candidate_workflows: Pick a specific capable user, design around that person's real cognitive limits, and give them control rather than protecting them from imagined misuse.
Architect hosted products for many small releases by making change boundaries explicit and cheap.
Let a real application drive platform abstractions, begin with a throwaway-scale implementation, and profile observed bottlenecks before optimizing.
Keep a single decision-maker able to take coherent design risks instead of averaging choices through a committee.

title: The Roots of Lisp
exclusion_reason: A short introduction to Lisp's semantic core and historical origin that points elsewhere for the complete article; it offers no specific reusable startup, product, team, or work process.

title: The Other Road Ahead
candidate_workflows: Release one small change at a time, test the changed surface, observe production immediately, and fix fresh defects before they can combine with later changes.

Put support beside product development, treat every genuine complaint as high-value evidence, reproduce it from live state, and route confusing behavior as product research rather than support overhead.
Give trusted makers clear ownership, keep the team small, and choose the next project by current expected user value instead of a long speculative roadmap.

When choosing hosted delivery, budget for continuous operational ownership: the makers must monitor recent changes and own the software/infrastructure boundary, and the team must account for combined development and on-call stress because the product never reaches a final ship point.
Watch real users complete the product's activation path, locate the exact abandonment step, make the smallest clarifying change, and measure completion and revenue effects immediately.
Launch with low fixed costs, make trial and purchase nearly frictionless, start with flexible smaller customers, and use subscription economics to fund continuous improvement.

title: What Made Lisp Different
exclusion_reason: A historical catalog of nine technical ideas introduced by Lisp and their later adoption; it does not turn that catalog into a reusable founder or product decision process.

title: Why Arc Isn't Especially Object-Oriented
candidate_workflows: Before adopting a pervasive architecture, identify the domains where it maps naturally, separate the capabilities you need from the full paradigm, and reject justifications based only on popularity or enterprise process.
Prefer adding an abstraction in response to demonstrated use over including it because convention labels it a good idea.

title: Taste for Makers
candidate_workflows: Critique a product by stripping ornament until the real problem is visible, checking that the interaction matches human use, and replacing a difficult formulation with an equivalent tractable one when possible.
Give users a small set of composable primitives instead of prescribing every outcome.
Plan to discard and redraw early work, make mistakes easy to acknowledge and fix, and choose media and tools that keep change cheap.

Choose or create a concentrated environment where talented people work on related problems; treat proximity to an active center of work as a major input to individual output, not as a substitute for talent.

After developing domain expertise, use persistent dissatisfaction with tolerated flaws as a problem-discovery signal; study the best prior solutions and optimize for correctness over forced originality.

title: What Languages Fix
candidate_workflows: Compare technical products by stating in one sentence the predecessor problem each fixes; use the resulting map to distinguish variants addressing technical or user limitations from those motivated by platform control.

title: Succinctness is Power
candidate_workflows: Compare technical tools on the number of conceptual parts needed for representative real work, not superficial line counts; prefer tools that reduce the whole system's cognitive load.

Search repeated patterns for an abstraction that shortens many cases, then validate the claimed leverage on substantial field projects and open-ended discovery rather than only short predefined benchmarks.
Evaluate local cleverness against total system readability, requiring a repeated-use payoff before accepting a dense abstraction.

title: Revenge of the Nerds
candidate_workflows: Classify a project by problem difficulty, system control, library dependence, and realistic hiring scale, then choose the most powerful suitable tool instead of defaulting to the industry median.
Make technical and product decisions for user outcomes rather than investor or acquirer comfort; treat orthodoxy as a risk factor when it erases the advantage that makes the product valuable.
Attack a hard problem where better abstractions compound, use a small expert team, and build bottom-up domain primitives to reduce code and coordination.

title: A Plan for Spam
candidate_workflows: For a classification product, assemble labeled positive and negative corpora, combine measurable evidence probabilistically instead of accumulating hand rules, and tune thresholds around the real asymmetry between error types.
Turn user corrections into individualized training data so the product improves with actual use and becomes harder for an adversary to tune against a universal rule set.
Red-team an adaptive system by assuming the adversary knows the method, then prefer feedback-driven defenses that continue learning as attacks change.
Maintain a clean evaluation corpus and add an independent second-stage safeguard when rare false positives carry disproportionate harm.

title: Design and Research
candidate_workflows: Name the intended user, observe what that person needs rather than merely recording requested features, and judge the design by the user's outcome.
Put a rough prototype in front of actual users quickly, refine that same artifact toward production, and preserve an always-working state that gives the team short feedback and motivation cycles.
Collect advice from trusted peers, then leave the final product decision with one accountable owner so the design remains coherent.
